name: memory-save
description: 'Saves, corrects, or forgets one lasting fact in the project''s memory, or sends it to the record where it belongs. Use when the owner says "remember this", "from now on", "forget that", or "remind me" with no time given, corrects the agent, or a hook says a save is due.'
---

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Saves, corrects, or retires one fact in the project's memory with `toolkit memory` commands, or sends the fact to its proper home. It never edits memory files by hand. Memory keeps one record per concept (for example `feedback_ways_of_working`, `project_billing`), with one `##` section per fact; an `event_` record holds one episode.

## Steps

Track these steps in the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

1. Decide the home with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory, which wins; otherwise `references/memory-criteria.md`). Not memory: send it to its home ("Where other things go" below) and stop.
2. Find the concept it belongs in, and any section that already holds it. List the concepts of its type (title, summary, updated date), search, and read each likely concept whole, with its version. The save's duplicate check compares wording, so only this search finds a section the new fact contradicts (for example "Mondays" against "Tuesdays").
   `toolkit memory list --type <type>`
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
   `toolkit memory get <key> --json`
3. Read the approval mode and apply "Approval policy" below. When it says ask, ask and wait.
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
4. Pick where it goes ("Choosing the concept" below), write the section text in the record format (`references/record-format.md`), and save with the form for the case ("Save forms" below).
5. Exit code 2 saved nothing. Read the "Error:" line. "Belongs in the concept <key>": add it there with the command the "Fix:" line prints, or, when it is a different concept, save again with `--new-concept`. Records listed: the duplicate check. "Changed since it was read": read it again and redo the change. Any other rule: fix the text as the message says. `references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 2, has each case.
6. "Forget that" right after a section save: run the "Undo:" command the save printed (it removes that section). About a whole concept: retire it, with his words as the reason. Delete only when his own words say delete ("Approval policy").
   `toolkit memory retire <key> --reason '<his words>'`
7. An owner to-do with no work item, or a change to what is happening now: update the current focus (`references/current-focus.md`). A project term: update the glossary (`references/glossary.md`).
8. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
9. Read the record back, check, and reply in one line ("Replies" below). End with the question still waiting for the owner, or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Approval policy

This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy.

- The owner's own words are the approval: "remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", or a correction. Save now, with `--approved-by <owner>`. That includes a fact about a named person he asks you to remember ("remember that Priya's last day is October 15").
- `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first, in exactly this form: "Save to memory: <one-line summary>?". Save after his yes (`references/proposals.md` when a proposal was saved for the question).
- A preference or fact he mentions in passing, without a keep phrase or an instruction ("screenshots were more useful than the text"), is inferred: ask "Save to memory: ...?" first. Only his keep words, or his yes to that question, are an approval.
- Recommend a yes only with evidence from this project (what he said, what happened, and when). With none, ask without a recommendation.
- `trusted` mode: a routine fact the agent is sure of is saved without asking and reported in one line, with no approver. The record says "Trusted grant".
- In either mode, always ask first for anything about a named person or personal details that he did not ask you to remember, for more than five records at once, and for a change to this policy.
- A delete needs his own words about that record ("delete it", "remove it for good"), or his yes to a numbered list that shows the delete. Do not ask again: the host asks him to confirm `toolkit memory delete`, and that prompt is the confirmation. "Forget that" is a retire, never a delete.
- A yes covers only the change and the meaning shown. Silence is never a yes.
- `--approved-by` is only for a change his words or his yes covered. Give his name exactly as the project settings hold it (`project.owner`, for example "Mike Rihm", not "Mike").
- A concept's `authorization` line is the approval of the concept. A section save never changes it; when the save's approval differs, the CLI records it on that section's Evidence and limits line (`references/record-format.md`, "Frontmatter").
- An unanswered "Save to memory?" stays a proposal until he answers (`references/proposals.md`). Never drop it, and never save it with an approver.
- Only the owner switches the mode, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date, then run one of:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`

## Choosing the concept

- One concept is one subject a future session would look up as a whole: how he wants the agent to work (`feedback_ways_of_working`), the billing setup (`project_billing`), his role and habits (`user_profile`), where dashboards live (`reference_dashboards`).
- The fact has the concept's type. Add it to the existing concept of that type whose title and summary cover it, as a new section. The heading names the sub-topic in a few words ("Force-push", "Refund window").
- The concept already has a heading for this sub-topic: add under it with `--append`. The fact corrects what a section says: replace that section with `--expect`.
- No concept of that type covers it: start a new one. Its slug and title name the concept, not the fact (`project_billing`, not `project_invoices_go_out_on_the_1st`), and its summary says what the whole concept covers.
- An event is always its own record: one episode per `event_` record.
- Two concepts fit: pick the one a future session would open first, and link the other from the section's **Related memories** line.

## Save forms

`<file>` is `-` in Claude Code, with the body on standard input after a quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`). In Codex give `--body '<text>'` in place of `--body-file <file>`. `references/record-format.md` shows both.

The section text (`<file>`) is the labels only: no `# ` title and no `##` heading; `--section` gives the heading.

- A new fact for an existing concept, from the owner's words or his yes:
  `toolkit memory save --concept <key> --section '<heading>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
- A new concept, with its first fact:
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <concept-slug> --description '<one-line summary of the concept>' --section '<heading>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
- In `trusted` mode, a routine fact the agent is sure of: either form without `--approved-by`.
- A question he has not answered yet: either form with `--proposal` in place of `--approved-by`. With `--concept`, `--description` is the fact in one line; the concept changes only after his yes.
- A correction of one section read in step 2, which his words or his yes covered:
  `toolkit memory save --concept <key> --section '<heading>' --body-file <file> --expect <version> --approved-by <owner>`
- One more fact under a heading the concept already has: add `--append` to the first form.
- The concept's summary no longer covers it: add `--description '<new summary>'` to a section save.
- An event (its own record):
  `toolkit memory save --type event --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
- A whole record rewritten (rare; read it with `--json` first):
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --expect <version> --approved-by <owner>`
- A new record that replaces an old one: add `--supersedes <old-key>` to a new-record form.
- A better name, or a type that matches the content:
  `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script. In Codex a joined command runs inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight, Notion, and the main checkout's `.memory/`.
- Put one-line values (`--description`, `--source`, `--reason`) in single quotes. An apostrophe inside them: Claude Code writes `'\''`; Codex writes ’ (U+2019) or rewords, and never uses `'\''`, which runs the command inside the sandbox. Double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`, drop that text, and the save still says "Saved".
- Never use a fixed file name such as `/tmp/memory.md`, and never write a file and run the command in one shell command.
- Body labels are bold paragraphs (`**Remember:**`), never `## Remember` headings. A `##` heading names a sub-topic; the CLI writes it from `--section`.
- A save that starts a new file for a fact whose words match an existing concept is refused with "belongs in the concept <key>". Read that concept before adding `--new-concept`.
- Replacing a section, and removing one, need `--expect <version>` from a `--json` read; adding a section does not.
- **Why** is the owner's reason in his words, or exactly "Not stated by the owner." Never a reason you inferred.
- In `onboarding` mode, a save with neither `--approved-by` nor `--proposal` is stored as "No approval recorded" (a section save: "Saved on <date> with no approval recorded." on that section's Evidence and limits line), and the save prints a "Note:" line about it. That is a mistake: fix it at once. Ask him, then save again with `--expect` and `--approved-by` after his yes, or with `--proposal` while he has not answered.
- A whole-record save of an existing key without `--expect` saves nothing. Take the version from the `--json` read; the first 12 characters are enough. Keep that read: its old text is the undo for an update.
- Add `--allow-similar` only after reading every record the duplicate check listed.
- A proposal the Stop hook saved holds only the one-line summary. His plain yes is `toolkit memory approve`, which takes out its "Do not rely on this" words. A proposal that names no concept also needs `--concept <type>_<subject>`: the concept its fact goes in, an existing one or a new key named for its subject (with `--title` and `--description`). When he adds a reason or a detail, approve it first, then save its section with his words (`references/proposals.md`).
- Never store email addresses, secrets, or work-item status. The CLI catches common secret shapes, not all. For a secret, save where it is kept, never the secret.
- Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- Say "proposal" only for a record saved with `--proposal` (by you or the Stop hook). When nothing was saved, say that nothing was saved, and ask.
- An inferred fact whose home is a project document (for example `PROJECT.md`) is asked the same way, as one yes-or-no line: "Add to PROJECT.md: <one line>?". When he does not answer, add it to the current focus under "Waiting on the owner", so it is asked again (`references/current-focus.md`).
- The host refused `toolkit memory delete` without asking him (Codex with approvals off): the cause is that approval setting. Show him the exact command to run in a terminal and wait. Do not retire the record in its place unless he asks for that.
- Built-in memory: the CLI rebuilds `MEMORY.md` and repairs links in other notes after a rename, supersede, retire, or delete, and names each note it changed. Read that report (`references/memory-builtin.md`).

## Where other things go

| The owner's words are about | Home | Open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project work, a task, a bug, "add it to the backlog" | A work item | `work-on` |
| A decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md` | `work-decide` |
| A requirement for a work item | The item's requirements | `work-requirements` |
| Behavior already delivered | `requirements/` | none |
| How a change is built | The item's design | `solution-design` |
| Verified current structure of the system | `system-guide/` | none |
| Outside documentation | `ai-external-knowledge/` | none |
| A standing rule for how agents work here | A rule-file change, proposed to him | none |
| His to-do with no work item and no time | Current focus, Untracked to-dos | step 7 |
| A to-do with a time ("at 9 tomorrow") | A scheduled reminder, outside memory | the host's scheduling tool |
| A project term | The glossary | step 7 |

A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy the record's body.

## Replies

Use these lines word for word, with the record's title, also when the memory line is one part of a longer reply. `toolkit memory save`, `approve`, and `reject` print the filled line ("Reply line for the owner, word for word"): copy it. Every memory reply ends with the next step: the question still waiting for the owner (for example "Save to memory: <one line>?"), or the exact words that continue. Never end on what was not done ("I haven't saved anything.").

- A new record or a new section: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." For a section, the title is "<heading> (in <concept title>)". His "forget that" right after a section save is the "Undo:" command the save printed.
- An update: "Updated in memory: <title>. Say 'undo that' to put back the old wording." His "undo that" is a save of the old text from the `--json` read, or of the old section text (`previous`) (`references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 3). Right after a supersede, the undo is a restore of the old record and a retire of the new one (same file, section 4).
- A removed section: "Removed from memory: <heading> (in <concept title>). Say 'undo that' to put it back."
- A proposal: "Saved as a proposal for your yes or no: <title>."
- A rejected proposal: "Not saved: <title>. I will not suggest it again.", then the next step.
- A retire: "Retired from memory: <title>. Say 'bring it back' to restore it." His "bring it back" is the whole restore in `references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 7, not `toolkit memory restore` alone.
- A delete: "Deleted from memory, as you said: '<his words>'. This cannot be undone." For a secret or an email address, add that older backups still hold it (`references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 8).
- A failed save: lead with "Not saved: <reason>." Keep the text and try again later in the session. With Hindsight or Notion, the command prints the fix (`references/memory-hindsight.md`, `references/memory-notion.md`).

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds one line when the owner's message holds one of six keep phrases: "remember that" (or "remember this"), "from now on", "don't ever", "note that", "going forward", or "keep in mind". It is a reminder: route the fact with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase got no save, work-item change, or decision in the turn. Save it, or say in one line where it went instead.
- Ask in exactly the form "Save to memory: <one line>?" (bold is fine). Other wording, such as "Save it to memory?", makes the Stop hook stop the turn once and ask for that form.
- When a reply asks "Save to memory: <summary>?" and no proposal was saved in that turn, the Stop hook tries to save one, and the next turn's context says what happened:
  - It saved a proposal and names its key: his yes approves that key, his no rejects it (`references/proposals.md`, "Recording the owner's answer").
  - Memory already holds a proposal like it, and names it: his answer approves or rejects that proposal.
  - It saved a proposal for an existing concept ("for the concept <key>"): his yes adds the fact to that concept as a section.
  - Memory already holds a record about the same subject, and names it: read it as in step 2. The same fact: keep it, or update it with `--expect`. A different fact and his yes: add it to that concept as a section, or save it with `--allow-similar` and `--approved-by`. Never overwrite a record with a different fact.
  - The text looks like a secret, so nothing was saved: never save it; after his yes, save only where the secret is kept.
  - The save failed: save the proposal yourself in this turn, with `--proposal`.

| `references/toolkit-commands.md` | A `toolkit` command fails, is refused by a hook, or you are unsure how to pass text in this host |

# Humanize Anything Sent to Another Person

Any text that will leave the project and be read by someone other than the owner
is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,
chat messages, support case text and comments, GitHub issues, pull request
descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.
# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.
# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. An unanswered save question is kept as a proposal: the agent does not rely on it, and `work-decide` shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it. The `memory-save` skill says how.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the owner says he is clearing context or ending the session, or asks for a handoff, use the `handoff` skill, whatever the session's length. When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip the offer for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): skip `git fetch`, and never report a fetch failure as a blocker.
- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

# Local project memory

Keep future sessions oriented without turning every conversation into lasting memory. This folder is the project's built-in memory store and can be opened directly as an Obsidian vault. Active topics stay flat; filenames and YAML types agree. Git ignores this folder, so back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>`.

## Read and route

- Read `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` at startup; the session briefing includes it. Read `MEMORY.md` as a short index, then open relevant topics and read each one whole. Check dates, scope, and the current source before acting on a remembered claim.
- Read `memory-criteria.md` before selecting or changing memory. It holds the default eligibility rules; the `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy and the onboarding or trusted mode. Use the terminology glossary for project language, including distinct meanings across systems.
- Link related notes inside this vault with relative Markdown links, such as `[account model](project_account_model.md)`. Obsidian shows backlinks to a note from the notes that link to it; a second reverse link is optional. Link only when the relationship helps retrieval, and check that the target exists. Keep tracker URLs and paths outside `.memory/` as source references rather than vault links.
- Keep current tasks and owner-mentioned to-dos in `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`, naming work items by ID. Keep full tasks, status, requirements, history, and the work item's design together in the chosen tracker; verified system behavior in the System Guide; procedures in instructions or skills; and raw outside sources in their source folders.

## Curate

- Keep one topic file per concept or area, such as `feedback_ways_of_working.md` or `project_billing.md`, with a `##` heading for each sub-topic. Allowed prefixes and matching `metadata.type` values are `user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, and `event`; an `event` file holds one episode. `project_topic_template.md` is a seed, not a saved memory. Each file starts with its title, a one-line summary (`description`), and the date of its last change (`updated`). Aim for a quick read; split a topic that grows too large.
- Record source and date, status, scope, the durable point, why it matters, and how to apply it. Keep uncertainty explicit. Preserve extra YAML fields written by a host or imported record.
- Search for the topic a new fact belongs to before creating one (`toolkit memory find`), and add the fact under a heading there (`toolkit memory save --concept <key> --section <heading>`). Create a new file only for a new concept. Correct, merge, or supersede in place where possible. Mark obsolete claims in both file text and index; do not leave an archived item reading as currently open.
- When renaming, merging, archiving, or deleting a topic, inspect links from other memory notes and repair any affected links, saving each repaired note with `toolkit memory save`. Do not leave a link pointing at a former active location.
- `toolkit memory save`, `retire`, and `restore` rebuild `MEMORY.md`; run `toolkit memory reindex` after any other topic change. The index holds one short line per active topic, grouped by prefix: its title, summary, and updated date, not the content itself. Keep it below the configured budget.
- Keep `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` under 50 lines by replacing stale sections, not appending, and write it with `toolkit memory focus --set-file`. Do not remove an unresolved owner to-do solely to meet that limit.
- Keep the glossary broad through sourced real terms, aliases, and system-specific meanings, and write it with `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. Do not invent definitions.

## Authority and completion

- Save through the `memory-save` skill, which holds the approval policy for onboarding and trusted mode. An explicit request to remember or correct is authorization for that specific change.
- Ask before ambiguous, bulk, or irreversible deletion of unique content. Only the owner can change the mode.
- A rejected candidate is not saved to another memory, a criteria example, the glossary, or a pending queue. Record only the general selection lesson, as a `feedback` memory, if the owner gave one.
- The main agent writes this folder only with `toolkit memory` commands, for example `save`, `retire`, `focus`, `glossary`, and `reindex` (`toolkit memory --help` lists them all). They lock the folder, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index. Never run parallel writers against the same topic.
- Read back changes with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor` before reporting success. Memory work does not edit requirements, work-item status, designs, deployments, or source code.
# Memory criteria

This file is the project-specific selection policy: what is worth keeping in lasting memory. The approval policy, including onboarding and trusted mode, is in the `memory-save` skill, which saves with `toolkit memory save`. When the owner corrects what is worth saving, save the correction as a `feedback` memory with `memory-save`, as a general rule, without copying the rejected memory. Those `feedback` memories override this page.

## Default test for lasting memory

Save a topic when it concerns this project, has a credible source, would matter in a future session, would be costly or unreliable to reconstruct, and has no better maintained owner. Prefer updating an existing topic: a new fact goes under a heading in the topic file for its concept, and a new file is only for a new concept. A short pointer to an authoritative record can qualify when future sessions would otherwise miss that record.

| Type and filename | Usually worth retaining | Route or reject instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_<topic>.md` | Relevant role, responsibility, working preference, or communication need the owner stated | Personal judgments, irrelevant biography, private details |
| `feedback_<topic>.md` | Repeated or standing correction to how the agent should work; confirmed selection lesson | One-off irritation, a rejected fact restated as policy, an instruction already in `AGENTS.md` |
| `project_<topic>.md` | Durable project constraint, rationale, technical landmark, or proven costly fix | A decision for the whole project (`DECISIONS.md`), code summary, schema copy, active ticket status, accepted requirement or design body |
| `reference_<topic>.md` | Hard-to-rediscover route to a source, system, dashboard, or decision record, with why to open it | Entire outside page or a path already obvious in `PROJECT.md` or the project map |
| `event_<topic>.md` | Significant project episode, one per file: what was done, what resulted, and where the output lives | Routine edit, tool call, raw error, daily progress log |

## Working context is different

`CURRENT_FOCUS.md` holds what is happening now: active work item IDs, what waits on the owner with no work item, untracked to-dos, and where the next session starts. It can change often. Keep a work item's detailed tasks and status in that item. Do not turn every open task into lasting memory. Do not discard an unresolved owner to-do merely to shorten the file.

## Never save as lasting memory

- Secrets, credentials, sensitive personal data, transcripts, scratch reasoning, raw logs, dropped guesses, or unsupported claims.
- A fact the same change already places in the authoritative file, unless a small route to that file is genuinely needed.
- Live status, pending approval, unshipped requirements, procedure steps, code restatements, or a current-system explanation that the code/System Guide owns.
- A rejected candidate under a new name or wider wording. A rejection stands until the owner changes it.

## Backup

This folder is Git-ignored. Back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>` and restore a fresh clone with `toolkit memory import --from <that folder>`. Linked worktrees resolve to one vault in the main checkout. A fresh clone or machine needs its memory restored before the agent treats an empty index as evidence that no memory exists.

# Memory record format

Purpose: the exact shape of one memory record (type, key, description,
frontmatter, and body), the same in built-in, Hindsight, and Notion memory.

## Contents

- One record per concept
- Types
- Keys and file names
- The description
- Frontmatter
- Body
- Links between records
- What never goes in a record
- Passing the body to the command
- Checklist before a save

The formats are the model project's: the topic template
(`.memory/project_topic_template.md`), `MEMORY.md`, `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`,
`memory-criteria.md`, and `terminology-glossary.md`. Only `toolkit memory`
commands write memory. They write the frontmatter from the flags; you write
the one-line description and the body.

## One record per concept

Memory keeps one record per concept or area, not one per fact (the owner's
decision of 2026-09-28). A concept is a subject a future session would look
up as a whole: how the owner wants the agent to work, the billing setup, the
deploy process. Examples: `feedback_ways_of_working`, `project_billing`,
`user_profile`, `reference_dashboards`.

- Each fact, or group of closely related facts, is one `## <Sub-topic>`
  section inside its concept, with the labels in "Body" below.
- A new fact goes into the concept it belongs to, as a new section or under
  an existing heading. A new record is only for a new concept.
- An `event_` record holds one episode. Events stay their own records.
- There are no starter concepts. A concept is created the first time a fact
  about it is saved.
- The top of every record gives its title (the `# ` line), a one-line summary
  (`description`), and the date of its last change (`updated`). The index and
  `toolkit memory list` show those three.
- A record written before this change holds one fact with no `##` section.
  It stays valid. `toolkit memory tidy --plan` proposes merging such records
  into concepts (the `memory-tidy` skill).

## Types

| Type | Holds | Example concept key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user` | Roles, responsibilities, working preferences, or communication needs the owner stated | `user_profile` |
| `feedback` | Standing corrections to how the agent works, and lessons about what to save | `feedback_ways_of_working` |
| `project` | Lasting project constraints, reasons, technical landmarks, or costly fixes, one area per concept | `project_billing`, `project_deploys` |
| `reference` | Hard-to-find routes to sources, systems, dashboards, or records, with why to open each | `reference_dashboards` |
| `event` | One significant project episode: what was done, the result, and where the output lives | `event_moved_off_heroku` |

Every section of a concept has the concept's type: a `feedback` fact goes
into a `feedback_` concept.

A type that does not match the content is fixed with
`toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`, never by saving a second record.

## Keys and file names

- `--name` is the slug: lower-case words joined by hyphens, naming the
  concept, for example `ways-of-working` or `billing`. The CLI refuses a slug
  over 60 characters; it never cuts one.
- The key is `<type>_<slug>` with every hyphen turned into an underscore:
  `--type feedback --name no-force-push` makes `feedback_no_force_push`.
  `toolkit memory save` prints the key it made.
- In built-in memory the key is also the file name without `.md` and the
  frontmatter `name`. The file name prefix and `metadata.type` always agree.
- Write a key with underscores everywhere: in `get`, `retire`, `restore`,
  `delete`, `--supersedes`, `--superseded-by`, and in a link. The CLI also
  finds a key typed with hyphens, but a link is text and must name the real
  file.

## The description

The concept's one-line summary: what a future session finds in it. Aim for
under 100 characters; the CLI refuses more than 150 and refuses more than one
line. Change it with `--description` when a new section changes what the
concept covers.

- Good: `How the owner wants the agent to work: questions, replies, Git habits`
- Too vague: `Preferences`

For an event, it is the one-line summary of the episode. For a proposal, it
is the one-line fact the owner is asked about.

## Frontmatter

The CLI writes it. Never write it by hand. A saved record starts like this:

```yaml
---
name: feedback_ways_of_working
description: "How the owner wants the agent to work: questions, replies, Git habits"
updated: 2026-09-28
metadata:
  type: feedback
status: current
source: The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26
last_verified: 2026-09-26
authorization: Approved by Mike on 2026-09-26
supersedes: none
---
```

| Field | Holds | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | The key | `--type` and `--name` |
| `description` | The concept's one-line summary | `--description` |
| `updated` | The date of the last change. Every save sets it; a link repair keeps it | The CLI |
| `metadata.type` | `user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, or `event` | `--type` |
| `status` | `current`; `needs-review` (also every proposal); `superseded` or `archived` for a retired record; `template` only on the seed template | `--proposal`, `retire`, `restore`, `approve` |
| `source` | Who or what said it, with an absolute date | `--source` |
| `last_verified` | The date the fact was last checked, or `unknown` | `--last-verified` |
| `authorization` | The approval of the concept: "Approved by <name> on <date>", "Trusted grant", "No approval recorded", or "Proposed by the agent on <date>". A section save never changes it (see below) | `--approved-by`, trusted mode, `--proposal` when the record is made, or saved whole |
| `supersedes` | The keys this record replaced (including records merged into it), or `none` | `--supersedes`, `merge` |
| `concept`, `section` | A proposal only: the concept and heading its fact goes to on the owner's yes | `--concept` with `--proposal` |

A save of an existing key keeps every field the command does not give again,
including fields another tool added. The CLI calls `superseded` and
`archived` together "retired" (`toolkit memory list --status retired`).

Each fact's approval: the concept's `authorization` line covers every
section that has no approval of its own. A section save (`--concept`),
`merge`, `split`, and `approve` never rewrite that line. When a fact's
approval differs from it, the CLI adds it to the end of that section's
**Evidence and limits** line, the way `--source` is recorded: "Approved by
Mike on 2026-09-28." or "Saved on 2026-09-28 with no approval recorded."
Replacing the section with the owner's approval takes the "no approval
recorded" words out.

## Body

The body starts with a `# <Title>` line: the concept's title. Then one
`## <Sub-topic>` section per fact or group of closely related facts. Each
section holds six labels, in this order, each in bold at the start of its own
paragraph. Never write a label as a heading such as `## Remember`; a `##`
heading names a sub-topic.

```markdown
# Ways of working

## Force-push

**Remember:** Never force-push to any branch in this repository.

**Why:** The owner lost a day of work to a force-push on 2026-09-12.

**How to apply:** Use a merge or a new commit instead. If a push is rejected, pull first.

**Evidence and limits:** The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26. Applies to every branch, including work-item branches.

**Related memories:** [pull requests](project_release_process.md#Pull%20requests)

**Authoritative records:** `DECISIONS.md` D-4; WI-012.

## Questions

**Remember:** Ask one requirements question at a time.

**Why:** Not stated by the owner.

**How to apply:** Put the question at the end of the reply text.

**Evidence and limits:** The owner, in chat, 2026-09-28.

**Related memories:** None.

**Authoritative records:** None.
```

- The heading names the sub-topic in a few words ("Force-push", "Deploy
  window"), never a label word. Use `###` for a heading inside a section.
- **Remember:** one lasting point, or a few closely related facts, with scope
  and date where they matter.
- **Why:** the owner's reason in his own words, or exactly "Not stated by the
  owner." Never a reason the agent inferred: a later answer would present it
  as his. This is deliberately narrower than the model's topic template,
  whose prompt asks why losing the context would change future work. The
  rule came from the fixes after the sample runs.
- **How to apply:** what a future agent checks or does with it.
- **Evidence and limits:** the source with an absolute date (`2026-09-26`,
  never "today" or "last week"), and any doubt or limit. Each section keeps
  its own, so where each fact came from stays clear.
- Write "None." after a label that has nothing. Never invent a related record
  to fill it.
- An event record has the same labels under its title, with or without a
  `##` section.

## Links between records

- Link a related record with a relative Markdown link to its file name:
  `[billing](project_billing.md)`. To point at one section, add `#` and the
  heading with each space written `%20`:
  `[deploy window](project_deploys.md#Deploy%20window)`. Obsidian opens that
  section. Never a `[[wikilink]]`.
- Link only when it helps a future session find the record, and check the
  target exists first (`toolkit memory get <key>`).
- Things outside memory (work item ids, `DECISIONS.md` rows, files in
  `requirements/` or `system-guide/`, tracker addresses) go under
  **Authoritative records** as plain text, not as links.
- Write the same links in every backend. The body text is the same
  everywhere, so a move between backends keeps them.
- The CLI repairs links to a record that is renamed, superseded, archived,
  deleted, merged into a concept (the link then goes to its section), or
  whose sections move to another concept (`split`), and names each record it
  changed. Read that report.

## What never goes in a record

- Secrets, passwords, keys, or email addresses. The CLI refuses the common
  shapes of a secret (an API key, a token, a private key, a password written
  out) in the description, the source, and the body, and an email address in
  `--source` and in the authorization. It does not catch every secret, or an
  email address in the body; those are the agent's job. When the owner wants
  a secret remembered, save where it is kept, never the secret: "The staging
  key is in 1Password under Staging".
- Work-item status, next steps, or unshipped requirements. The tracker owns
  them.
- A copy of a record that has a better home (a requirement, a design, a
  `DECISIONS.md` row). A short pointer under **Authoritative records** is
  allowed when a future session would otherwise miss that record.
- A fact the owner rejected, under the same or new words.

## Passing the body to the command

- Claude Code: pass it on standard input. Give `--body-file -`, then a quoted
  heredoc, then the body, then a line holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit memory save --concept feedback_ways_of_working --section 'Force-push' --body-file - --source 'The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26' --approved-by Mike <<'EOF'
  ```

- For one section (`--concept ... --section ...`) the text is that section
  only: the labels, with no `# ` title and no `##` heading of its own.

- Codex: give the body in single quotes with `--body '<text>'`. Newlines
  inside the quotes are kept. Write an apostrophe as ’ (the curly
  apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the text. Never `'\''` in Codex: the
  project's command rule does not match that form, so the command runs
  inside the sandbox, and the tool call can drop the backslash. For a long
  body, write a file with the file edit tool in a new folder made with
  `mktemp -d`, run the command alone with `--body-file <that file>`, then
  delete the file and the folder.
- One-line values (`--description`, `--source`) go in single quotes in both
  hosts. An apostrophe in them: Claude Code writes `'\''`; Codex writes ’ or
  rewords.
- Never write the file and run the command in one shell command, and never
  use a fixed name such as `/tmp/memory.md`.

## Checklist before a save

- [ ] The fact goes into the concept it belongs to; a new record only for
      a new concept. The concepts of a type: `toolkit memory list --type <type>`.
- [ ] The type matches the content (table above), and the concept's type.
- [ ] The section heading names the sub-topic in a few words.
- [ ] A new concept's slug names the concept, not one fact.
- [ ] The description is the concept's one-line summary (a proposal: the fact).
- [ ] Each section has all six bold labels, in order; a new concept also
      has its `# Title` line.
- [ ] **Why** holds the owner's words or "Not stated by the owner."
- [ ] Every date is absolute.
- [ ] Every link under **Related memories** points at a record that exists.
- [ ] No secret, email address, or work-item status.
